:::{#prp-population-mean-expectation}
#### The expectation of a randomly chosen unit's value is the average over the population

Let a population of $n$ units have values $\dsn{a}$,
which need not be distinct.
Let $U$ be one of the units $1, \ldots, n$ [chosen at random](probability-basics.qmd#def-random-choice),
and let $Y \eqdef a_U$ be its value.
Then the [expectation](#def-expectation) of $Y$ is the
[mean](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/linear-algebra-vectors.html#def-mean) of the values over the whole population:

$$\E{Y} = \avgin a_i$$

:::

::: proof

For each possible value $y$ of $Y$, let $n_y$ be the number of units whose value is $y$.

$$
\ba
\E{Y}
&= \sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} y \cd \P(Y = y)
&& \text{(definition of expectation)}
\\&= \sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} y \cd \frac{n_y}{n}
&& \text{(each unit is chosen with probability } 1/n \text{, and } n_y \text{ units have value } y \text{)}
\\&= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} \; \sum_{i : a_i = y} a_i
&& \text{(} y \cd n_y \text{ is the sum of the } n_y \text{ values equal to } y \text{)}
\\&= \avgin a_i
&& \text{(each unit has exactly one value, so the double sum counts every unit once)}
\ea
$$

When the values are distinct, every $n_y$ is $1$,
and the proposition reduces to @prp-mean-expectation.

:::
